definition.text: The particular set of environmental conditions and the role that a species or population occupies in its surroundings.

facts.text: The word was coined in 1910 by Roswell Hill Johnson, and Joseph Grinnell first used it in ecological research in 1917.
Grinnell's niche is set by the habitat a species lives in and the behaviours that let it persist and reproduce there.
In 1927 Charles Elton defined a niche by an animal's place in the living environment, especially its relations to food and enemies.
A niche can be described along many axes, including life history, habitat, position in the food chain and geographic range.
Once a niche is left empty, other organisms can fill it; introduced species may invade the niches of native organisms and outcompete them.
Every species evolved for a certain niche, so climate change, by shifting temperature and weather, puts species at risk.

definition.text: A view of the niche as a many-dimensional space whose axes are the conditions and resources a species needs for its population to persist.

facts.text: The zoologist G. Evelyn Hutchinson popularized this niche concept in 1957, asking why so many kinds of organisms live in one habitat.
His work led to ideas such as niche breadth, the variety of resources or habitats a species uses.
Turning a species' fundamental niche into a map of where it could live is the task of niche modelling.

definition.text: The fundamental niche is the full range of conditions a species could use without other species interfering; the realized niche is the narrower part it actually occupies.

facts.text: Pressure from other species, especially competition, usually squeezes a species into a narrower realized niche.
For example, a species able to live on a whole hillside may hold only its top because a stronger competitor excludes it lower down.
Similarly, a species' realized geographic range is a narrower subset of its fundamental range, limited by other species or barriers.

definition.text: The process by which competing species use their environment in different ways, which helps them live side by side.

facts.text: It is also called niche segregation, niche separation or niche partitioning.
Species that differentiate their niches compete less strongly and are more likely to coexist.
Resource partitioning is one form: some lizard species seem to coexist by eating insects of different sizes.
Differentiation can come from current competition, from past extinction of weaker competitors, or from species evolving different patterns of resource use.
Some species, such as a group of hispine beetles, share the same food and habitat with no evidence of niche differentiation.
Different plants living together can play complementary roles such as nutrient cycling and water regulation, a mechanism called niche complementarity.

definition.text: The rule that two species competing for the same limited resource cannot both persist at steady numbers.

facts.text: It is sometimes called Gause's law and summed up as 'complete competitors cannot coexist'.
A species with even a slight advantage dominates in the long run, so the weaker competitor dies out or shifts to a different niche.
Invasive species can drive native species locally extinct through competitive exclusion.
Ecologists Andrewartha and Birch argued that most natural populations rarely exhaust their resources, so too much weight on competition is wrong.

definition.text: The variety of ecosystems found within a region or across the whole planet.

facts.text: It covers both living features and non-living ones such as water and soil, and includes land and water ecosystems.
Globally it spans deserts, forests, grasslands, wetlands and oceans, and it is the largest scale of biodiversity.
Diverse ecosystems help supply oxygen, purify water and provide plants used as medicines.
Crop-pollinating insects are worth $14.6 billion a year to the US economy, and hand pollination would cost $5,715-$7,135 more per hectare.

definition.text: The study of how the living and non-living parts of an ecosystem interact as one integrated system.

facts.text: It focuses on functional processes such as primary production, decomposition and feeding relationships that keep ecosystems and their services going.
Eugene Odum and Howard T. Odum quantified flows of energy and matter through whole ecosystems.
Its findings have improved sustainable production of forage, fibre, fuel and water.
Most natural ecosystems are limited by nitrogen, and recycling of nutrients, mainly from decomposing plant litter, keeps them productive.
Intensive fertilizer use in the US Midwest has degraded fisheries in the Gulf of Mexico, showing that maximizing output can harm ecosystem processes.
In Guatemala's western highlands, forest loss has raised landslide and water-shortage risks, while Totonicapán, which kept its forests, is more economically stable.

definition.text: The two ways an ecosystem's structure is shaped: from below by how much energy plants bring in, and from above by predators.

facts.text: Trophic dynamics is the transfer of energy and nutrients between organisms.
Energy captured by plants passes to herbivores, then carnivores, then top carnivores, and the total energy shrinks at each higher level.
Predators can dramatically shift which species dominate on land and at sea; the balance of the two controls is a major research question.
Herbivory can speed litter decomposition and nutrient cycling by changing litter quality and vegetation.
Top carnivores keep herbivores in check; without them herbivores could multiply and eat all the plants.
If plant populations fall sharply, herbivores decline and then carnivores decline too.
An ecosystem need not be one or the other: a marine system may be bottom-up, then come under top-down control during fishing.
Correlations in abundance or biomass between consumers and resources are the evidence for bottom-up control, as when herbivore and detritivore biomass rises with primary productivity.

title: Ecosystem engineer

definition.text: A species that creates, substantially changes, maintains or destroys a habitat.

facts.text: Such species can strongly affect how many species an area holds and how varied its landscape is.
Beavers are the original example: by felling trees and building dams they change the distribution and abundance of many organisms.
Engineers matter because they modify resources, not because they are eaten; keystone species usually matter through feeding relationships instead.
By making habitats more varied, beavers can support species not found elsewhere, so conserving an engineer may protect a whole landscape's diversity.
Humans are thought to be the most dramatic ecosystem engineers, through cities, farming, logging, dams and mining.
Whales release nutrients at the surface that feed phytoplankton and spread them across oceans, a process called the 'whale pump'.
Introduced species such as kudzu and the zebra mussel often act as ecosystem engineers.
Ecosystem engineers can change how efficiently nutrients are recycled.

contested_note: Some ecologists see the term as a buzzword, since it may imply intent and every species changes its environment to some degree.
notes: Controversy sentences d68c4a17f10f, f939f45827db, d3d8a71d47f0 support the contested note.

definition.text: The two kinds of ecosystem engineer: allogenic ones change materials from one form to another, autogenic ones create habitat with their own bodies.

facts.text: Jones and colleagues identified the two types in 1994.
Woodpeckers are allogenic: the holes they carve in trees later house other birds and mammals.
Sphagnum moss is autogenic: it forms peatlands, and tree trunks likewise shelter lichens, mosses, squirrels, birds and insects.
Later work proposed six specific cases based on how species change materials and buffer physical forces.

definition.text: The branch of ecology that studies the roles, or functions, species play in their community or ecosystem.

facts.text: It emphasizes species' physiological, anatomical and life-history traits.
In his 1927 book Animal Ecology, Charles Elton proposed classifying ecosystem members by how they use resources, grouping similar users into 'guilds'.
From the 1970s guilds were renamed functional groups, and from the 1990s biodiversity came to be seen as a diversity of functions, not just of species.
Restorations with more functional diversity have shown lower levels of invasion by other species.

definition.text: The range and value of the traits of species and organisms that influence how an ecosystem works.

facts.text: Greater functional diversity raises an ecosystem's ability to regulate flows of energy and matter and to supply air, water and wood to people.
More diverse ecosystems are more resilient to extinctions, invasions, logging, farming and pollution.
The benefits scale non-linearly with diversity, and losing diversity disrupts ecosystems non-linearly too, especially across trophic levels.
Losing a single top predator can cascade down the food chain, reducing plant biomass and genetic diversity.
Functional extinction is the point at which a species no longer performs its historical role; endangered tigers, tuna and sea otters usually qualify.
Traits such as how an organism moves, gathers resources, reproduces or when it is active add to functional diversity.
Functional diversity raises ecosystem productivity by letting more niches be occupied.
Bees in managed landscapes show lower functional and species diversity than in natural habitats.

definition.text: A physical, physiological or seasonal trait that affects an organism's fitness indirectly through its growth, reproduction and survival.

facts.text: Counting too many traits can overestimate functional diversity, while too few can wrongly class vital species as redundant.
Traits are named by scale: individuals have ecophysiological and life-history traits, populations demographic traits, communities response traits and ecosystems effect traits.

definition.text: The set of resources and living and non-living conditions in a place that lets a particular species survive and reproduce.

facts.text: A species' habitat can be seen as the physical form of its ecological niche.
Physical factors include soil, moisture, temperature range and light; living factors include food supply and predators.
Generalist species thrive in many conditions, while specialists need a narrow set; the large blue butterfly lives only in chalk grassland where certain ants live.
Habitat types on land include forests, grasslands, wetlands and deserts; freshwater ones include rivers, lakes, marshes and bogs.
Loss of habitat is the single greatest threat to any species, and habitat destruction is the leading cause of biodiversity loss and extinction worldwide.
Protecting habitats, through national parks, reserves or limits on human activity, is a necessary step in maintaining biodiversity.
Monoculture tree plantations add tree cover but fail to provide the varied habitat most woodland creatures need.

definition.text: The small-scale physical conditions that a particular organism or population needs.

facts.text: Every habitat holds many microhabitats differing slightly in light, humidity, temperature and air movement.
Lichens on the north face of a boulder differ from those on its south face or top.
The more structurally varied a wood is, the more microhabitats it contains.

definition.text: Towns and cities as places where adaptable, generalist plants and animals make their homes.

facts.text: About 2,000 coyotes are thought to live in and around Chicago.
A twentieth-century survey of northern European homes found about 175 invertebrate species living inside them.

definition.text: The network of linked food chains in a community, showing who eats whom.

facts.text: Organisms are broadly classed as autotrophs, which make their own food, or heterotrophs, which feed on others.
Feeding links fall roughly into herbivory, carnivory, scavenging and parasitism.
Plants form the base level, and apex predators sit at the top where nothing kills them for food.
Energy flows one way through a food web, while materials such as nutrients cycle; eventually all the energy is lost as heat.
A food chain usually has at most four or five links, and aquatic chains are often longer than those on land.
Charles Elton's 1927 book Animal Ecology made food chains and food cycles central to ecology.
Losing one species can harm the whole chain, a knock-on loss called coextinction.

definition.text: A food web in which dead plant and animal matter is broken down by decomposers and passed on to detritivores and then carnivores.

facts.text: Detritus is any non-living organic matter, such as leaf litter, dead wood, carrion and dung.
Detrital and grazing webs connect: mushrooms from decomposers feed deer, squirrels and mice, and robins eat leaf-eating earthworms.

title: Food web complexity and stability

definition.text: The question of whether more complex food webs, with more species and links, are more stable.

facts.text: Connectance is the fraction of all possible feeding links that actually occur in a network.
Complexity is sometimes defined as the number of species multiplied by connectance, though this definition has been criticized.
Mathematical models challenged the idea that complexity brings stability, but later studies found it holds in real systems.

contested_note: Mathematical models suggested complexity does not bring stability, while later field studies supported the idea.

title: Trophic dynamics
article: Food web#Trophic dynamics and multitrophic interactions

definition.text: The study of how energy passes from one part of an ecosystem to another through feeding.

facts.text: Raymond Lindeman introduced the trophic level concept in a landmark 1942 paper on trophic dynamics.
Assigning organisms to one level is imprecise, since omnivores feed at several levels.
Research finds distinct levels exist, but above the herbivores food webs are better described as a tangle of omnivores.

title: Keystone species

definition.text: A species whose effect on its surroundings is far larger than its numbers would suggest.

facts.text: The zoologist Robert T. Paine introduced the concept in 1969.
Like the keystone of an arch, it may be a small part of the ecosystem by biomass, yet removing it can trigger a dramatic shift.
When Paine removed ochre starfish from rock pools, mussels took over: 15 clinging species fell to 8 within three years, and ten years later mussels largely filled the pools.
When fur hunting cut sea otters to fewer than 1000 in the north Pacific, sea urchins grazed away the kelp forests; reintroducing otters restored them.
Removing gray wolves from Greater Yellowstone led to overgrazing that hurt beavers and streams; after wolves returned, the riparian ecosystem recovered within a few years.
Keystone mutualists matter through helpful partnerships: some seeds will not grow unless they have passed through a cassowary.
The concept overlaps with flagship, indicator and umbrella species, and has helped ecologists communicate with conservation policymakers.
One researcher listed 230 species called keystones in about 157 studies over the 50 years since Paine's paper.

contested_note: Critics say the term oversimplifies complex ecosystems, has been stretched to many different meanings, and depends on local context.

definition.text: The making of organic compounds from carbon dioxide in air or water, mainly by photosynthesis.

facts.text: Almost all life on Earth relies directly or indirectly on primary production.
The organisms that do it, called primary producers or autotrophs, form the base of the food chain: mainly plants on land and algae in water.
A small share is driven by chemosynthesis, which takes energy from chemical reactions of inorganic compounds instead of light.
On land it depends mainly on water and temperature, and it is strongly limited in deserts and polar regions.
Satellite estimates put Earth's total primary production at 104.9 petagrams of carbon per year, 56.4 on land and 48.5 in the oceans.
Human societies are part of Earth's primary production cycle but influence it disproportionately.

title: Gross and net primary production
article: Primary production#Gross primary production and net primary production

definition.text: Gross primary production is all the chemical energy producers capture in a given time; net primary production is what remains after they use some for their own respiration.

facts.text: Net primary production is what is available for producers' growth and reproduction, and so for herbivores to eat.
Net primary productivity equals gross primary productivity minus the carbon producers lose through cellular respiration.
Gross production is harder to measure than net, because respiration constantly uses up some of the sugars produced.
Estimates scaled up from eddy covariance measurements give a land gross primary production of 123±8 Gt of carbon per year for 1998-2005.
NPP is calculated as gross primary production minus respiration.
Most primary production comes from photosynthesis, using sunlight, water and CO2.
Where there is no light, as in groundwater, caves and hydrothermal vents, lithoautotrophs using chemicals such as hydrogen sulfide or methane are the only producers.
Net ecosystem production subtracts the respiration of both autotrophs and heterotrophs from gross primary production.

definition.text: The making of organic matter in the sea, carried out almost entirely by algae.

facts.text: It happens in the photic zone, a sunlit surface layer about 10-100 m thick.
Sinking particles constantly remove nutrients from the sunlit layer, which are replaced only when deeper water mixes or wells up.
Where wind-blown desert dust does not reach, as in the Southern and North Pacific oceans, lack of iron limits production, creating high-nutrient, low-chlorophyll regions.

definition.text: An organism's position in a food web, counted as the number of feeding steps it is from the start of the chain.

facts.text: Level 1 is primary producers such as plants, level 2 herbivores, level 3 or higher carnivores, and apex predators typically sit at level 4 or 5.
Organisms get food in three basic ways: as producers, consumers or decomposers.
Herbivores are primary consumers, carnivores that eat them are secondary consumers, and carnivores that eat carnivores are tertiary consumers.
Raymond Lindeman developed the concept in 1942, building on August Thienemann's 1926 terms producers, consumers and reducers.
Consumers convert on average only about 10% of the energy in their food into their own tissue, so food chains rarely exceed 5 or 6 levels.
Plants turn about 1% of the sunlight they receive into chemical energy, so only about 0.001% of it ends up in a tertiary consumer.
Fish at higher trophic levels usually fetch more money, which can lead to overfishing at those levels.
Humans have a mean trophic level of about 2.21, about the same as a pig or an anchovy.

title: Fractional trophic level

definition.text: A trophic level that need not be a whole number, because many organisms feed at more than one level.

facts.text: A consumer's trophic level is one plus the diet-weighted average trophic level of what it eats.
Most fish and other marine consumers fall between 2.0 and 5.0; 5.0 occurs in apex predators such as polar bears and orcas.
Trophic level can be measured from stable nitrogen isotopes in tissues, which rise about 3–4‰ at each level.

distinct_from: Mean trophic level of fisheries catch

title: Mean trophic level of fisheries catch

definition.text: The average trophic level of all the fish caught in an area or ecosystem in a given year, used to track fishing pressure.

facts.text: Early reports found steep declines in it, a process called fishing down the food web.
Pauly and colleagues report it peaked at 3.4 in 1970 in the northwest and west-central Atlantic and fell to 2.9 by 1994, as catches shifted from cod and haddock to shrimp and herring.
Pauly and others built the Fisheries in Balance (FiB) index in 2000 to check whether falling trophic levels are matched by rising catches.

contested_note: Later work found mean trophic levels in catches and surveys have not declined globally, suggesting fishing down the food web is not worldwide.

definition.text: An interaction linking three trophic levels at once, such as plant, herbivore and predator.

facts.text: Studying only two levels at a time can mislead, because plants and predators together can shape herbivore population growth.
Plant shape can change how well a plant resists herbivores by affecting the herbivores' enemies.

definition.text: The science of conserving nature and Earth's biodiversity, aiming to protect species, habitats and ecosystems from excessive extinction.

facts.text: It is interdisciplinary, drawing on natural and social sciences and on natural resource management, and reaches into law, economics and philosophy.
The field took its name from the First International Conference on Research in Conservation Biology, held in 1978 in La Jolla, California.
Because natural systems are declining fast, it is often called a 'discipline with a deadline'.
Conservation is either in-situ, protecting a species in its natural habitat, or ex-situ, outside it, such as in gene banks.
Conservation biologists have begun working with economists to measure nature's wealth and services, an accounting approach called natural capital.
The global extinction rate may be about 1,000 times higher than the natural background rate.
Some conservationists follow a resource ethic of the greatest good for the most people, while others argue nature has intrinsic value apart from its usefulness.

definition.text: A species with narrow ecological needs whose condition is watched as a sign of an ecosystem's health.

facts.text: Amphibians, with permeable skin and ties to wetlands, are very sensitive to environmental harm and can act as a 'miner's canary'.
They are monitored to detect damage from pollution or other human activity, and can guide changes in practice such as forestry methods.
Monitoring several indicators, from genes to landscapes, is generally recommended.

definition.text: A species whose protection also shelters many other species and habitats because it needs a large area.

facts.text: The monarch butterfly migrates across North America through many ecosystems, so protecting it protects much else.
Umbrella species often double as flagship species, such as the giant panda or tiger, that capture public attention.
Conservation bias towards flagship species can sometimes threaten other species of greater concern.

definition.text: A step-by-step way of choosing and designing reserves to protect the highest-priority biodiversity efficiently.

facts.text: Margules and Pressey set out six linked stages, from compiling biodiversity data and setting goals to selecting new areas and maintaining their value.
Planners generally use geographic information systems to support decisions.

definition.text: A summary of the main threats to biodiversity: habitat loss, invasive species, pollution, human population and overharvesting.

facts.text: The primary threats are habitat destruction, such as deforestation and urban growth, and overexploitation, such as wildlife trade.

definition.text: A broad philosophy and social movement that seeks to protect living things, habitats and the wider environment.

facts.text: It advocates preserving, restoring and improving the natural environment, including systems such as the climate, and is often a movement to control pollution or protect biodiversity.
At its core it tries to balance people's relations with the natural systems they depend on so that all are sustainable.
The movement began as a response to rising smoke pollution during the Industrial Revolution; Britain's Alkali Acts of 1863 were the first large-scale modern environmental laws.
The 1972 UN Conference on the Human Environment in Stockholm, attended by 113 nations, led to the UN Environment Programme.
Its strands include free-market, evangelical and labour environmentalism and the conservation movement, and it gave rise to green parties.
Critics say early environmentalism reflected mostly white middle- and upper-class interests and overlooked indigenous communities and nearby low-income residents.
Every year more than 100 environmental activists are murdered worldwide.

title: Free-market environmentalism

definition.text: The view that free markets, property rights and tort law are the best tools for keeping the environment healthy and sustainable.

facts.text: It treats stewardship as natural and relies on individual and class-action lawsuits to drive out polluters.
Its advocates argue that clear, protected property rights let parties negotiate better environmental outcomes and sue to stop harm.
They blame environmental problems on laws that obscure property rights and on transaction costs too high for bargaining.
Critics say it cannot handle collective problems, since resources such as water are hard to privatize and pollution is hard to trace.

contested_note: Critics argue market tools cannot handle collective environmental problems, while proponents see property rights as the best remedy.
notes: Assigned to this ecology chapter by the concept graph but belongs with the economics chapters (externalities, property rights).

definition.text: Trade unions' work to shape environmental policy, campaign on environmental issues and partner with environmental groups.

facts.text: Unions face a dilemma between the economic growth model and the global ecological crisis.
To promote green jobs, unions developed the idea of a just transition.

definition.text: Ideas and actions opposing environmentalism as a whole or particular environmental policies.

facts.text: It can take the form of an organized countermovement targeting climate science and environmental regulation.
Its actors may include workers in industries threatened by environmental policy and anti-environmentalist think tanks.

definition.text: The practice of protecting wild species and their habitats to keep wildlife populations healthy and restore natural ecosystems.

facts.text: Major threats include habitat destruction and fragmentation, overexploitation, poaching, pollution, climate change and illegal wildlife trade.
The IUCN estimates that over 42,100 assessed species are at risk of extinction, and a 2019 UN report put the figure for all species at a million.
More than 80% of the world's species live in forests, so deforestation is a major threat.
The illegal wildlife trade is estimated to be worth 7-23 billion, with around 100 million plants and animals traded a year.
In 1973 the US passed the Endangered Species Act, and CITES was agreed internationally to stop global trade in endangered wildlife.
Habitat conservation protects a whole habitat to protect the species in it, often preferable when many endangered species share it.
Monitoring populations lets managers track threatened species and test whether management works.

definition.text: The study of genetic factors that affect whether a species can be conserved.

facts.text: High genetic diversity improves survival because it gives more capacity to adapt to future change.
Low diversity brings inbreeding depression and drift, reducing adaptability and raising genetic problems.
By the early 1990s only 20-25 Florida panthers remained, highly inbred and suffering kinked tails, heart defects and low fertility.

definition.text: The non-living chemical and physical parts of the environment that affect living things and how ecosystems work.

facts.text: They include water, light, temperature, humidity, acidity, salinity, altitude, minerals, tides, dissolved oxygen and soil.
Humans can create or change them: fertilizers alter habitats and greenhouse gases change the ocean's pH.
Differences in them, such as water availability between rainforests and deserts, set limits on which species can live where and shape competition.
Factors such as salinity can give one species a competitive edge over another, creating pressure that leads to new species.

definition.text: A predator at the top of a food chain that has few or no natural predators of its own.

facts.text: Apex predators occupy the highest trophic levels; on land chains are shorter, so wolves mostly eat large herbivores that eat plants.
They are central to how ecosystems function, to regulating disease and to maintaining biodiversity.
Predators that exert top-down control are often considered keystone species.
After gray wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone in 1995, elk declined and changed behaviour, letting willows, aspens and cottonwoods flourish and creating habitat for beavers and moose.
Humans have hunted many apex predators close to extinction, and climate change now threatens species such as the polar bear by shrinking Arctic sea ice.
Ecotourism sometimes relies on apex predators, and rewilding efforts have reintroduced species such as the Iberian lynx.
Reintroducing large predators is controversial, partly because farmers fear for their livestock.

definition.text: The rise in mid-sized predators that follows when the top predators that kept them in check are removed.

facts.text: Hunting of sperm whales, with a trophic level of 4.7, has increased populations of large squid.
In North America over the past two centuries, the ranges of all apex carnivores have shrunk while those of 60% of mesopredators have grown.
Removing badgers in a bovine tuberculosis trial more than doubled hedgehog densities.

verification.title: The Rise of the Mesopredator
verification.evidence: We also examine shifts in North American carnivore ranges during the past 200 years and show that 60% of mesopredator ranges have expanded, whereas all apex predator ranges have contracted.

title: Human trophic level

definition.text: The question of where humans sit in the food web, and whether they count as apex predators.

facts.text: A 2013 study averaged the trophic levels of foods in the human diet and found a mean of 2.21, from 2.04 in Burundi to 2.57 in Iceland.
That value is comparable to non-apex animals such as the anchovy or pig.
A 2014 critique found humans eating mainly predatory fish in two marine systems had trophic levels of 4.65 and 4.5, making them apex predators there.

contested_note: Ecologists disagree whether humans are apex predators, depending on whether land-based diets or marine food webs are measured.

definition.text: An organism that turns non-living energy sources, such as sunlight or chemicals, into energy stored in organic compounds that others can use.

facts.text: Autotrophs build carbohydrates, fats and proteins from carbon in simple substances such as carbon dioxide.
They are the producers in a food chain, such as plants on land and algae in water, and need no living source of carbon or energy.
Heterotrophs, including all animals and almost all fungi, depend on autotrophs for raw materials and fuel.
Plants can use only about 1% of the sun's energy for photosynthesis.
The German botanist Albert Bernhard Frank coined the term in 1892.
Researchers think the first cells were autotrophs, possibly living at deep-sea hydrothermal vents.

definition.text: An organism that makes its food using energy from chemical reactions of inorganic substances instead of light.

facts.text: They are often found at deep-ocean hydrothermal vents and include some archaea and bacteria.
They use substances such as hydrogen, iron, nitrogen and sulfur to generate energy.
In deep-sea vent ecosystems without sunlight, producers make food by chemosynthesis.

definition.text: The total mass of living organisms in a given area or ecosystem at a particular time.

facts.text: It can be measured as wet weight, dry weight, or the mass of organic carbon, depending on the context.
In 2018 Earth's live biomass was estimated at about 550 billion tonnes of carbon, mostly in plants.
Plants hold 450 billion tonnes of carbon and bacteria plus archaea 30, while animals make up less than 0.5% of the total.
By 2020 the mass of human-made materials was projected to surpass that of all living biomass on Earth.
On land biomass falls sharply at each higher trophic level, but in the oceans it can increase at higher levels.
Ocean producers account for almost half of yearly production but only about 0.2% of total biomass.
The biomass of wild land mammals is believed to be seven times lower than prehistoric values, while livestock biomass exceeds that of all wild mammals.

definition.text: A large geographical region with a distinctive climate, vegetation and animal life.

facts.text: A biome's community forms in response to its physical environment and regional climate.
The International Biological Program of 1964–74 popularized the concept.
Boundaries between biomes must be drawn somewhat arbitrarily because one biome changes gradually into the next.
Climate change could shift biomes so much that between 54% and 22% of land will have climates matching other biomes, and 3.6% entirely new ones.
Woody plant encroachment, which turns grass savanna into shrub savanna, is an example of a biome shift.

verification.title: Protected-area targets could be undermined by climate change-driven shifts in ecoregions and biomes
verification.evidence: Here we use spatial climate analogs to examine potential climate-driven shifts in terrestrial ecoregions and biomes under a +2 °C warming scenario and associated implications for achieving 30% area-based protection targets.
verification.note: nearly a quarter of land shifts biome matches 22%; 30% is the protection target

definition.text: The various systems ecologists use to divide the world's land into biome types, mostly by temperature and rainfall.

facts.text: In 1947 Leslie Holdridge classified climates by the effects of temperature and rainfall on vegetation.
Whittaker's scheme, using precipitation and temperature, simplified Holdridge's and is easier to use but less specific.
A WWF team divided the world into biogeographic realms and ecoregions, each with a main biome, and used it to pick the Global 200 conservation priorities.
The many competing schemes show that biomes do not fit neatly into any classification.

title: Anthropogenic biome

definition.text: A way of describing the land biosphere as it now is, divided into units shaped by lasting human use such as farming, settlement and forestry.

facts.text: Across much of Earth, crops, rangelands and cities have replaced the vegetation conventional biome systems predict.
Erle Ellis and Navin Ramankutty first named and mapped anthromes in 2008.
By 2000, over half of Earth's ice-free land had been turned into rangelands, croplands, villages and dense settlements.
While 23.4% of remote woodland anthrome is protected, only 2.3% of irrigated village anthrome is.

contested_note: Sources describe an open debate over whether urban areas should be treated as a unique biome.

definition.text: A chain of secondary extinctions set off when a key species in an ecosystem dies out.

facts.text: Species most at risk depend on a few foods, rely on the lost species, or must live alongside an invasive species.
The main cause is loss of top predators, which lets prey multiply, overuse their food and then crash.
Hunting sea otters for pelts let urchins strip the kelp, leaving barrens where urchins and kelp-dependent species died out locally.

definition.text: A group of populations of different species living in the same area at the same time.

facts.text: It is also called a biocoenosis, biotic community or ecological community.
Community ecology studies how coexisting species interact, and their distribution, structure and abundance.
Each species occupies a niche, and having different niches lets species coexist.
Some species, such as foundation species, keystone species and ecosystem engineers, have outsized influence, and losing them often destabilizes the community.
Community structure is often measured through networks such as food webs.

definition.text: Two opposing views of what a community is: a tightly linked unit, or a loose set of species each responding to conditions on its own.

facts.text: Frederic Clements saw the community as a kind of superorganism with sharp boundaries.
Henry Gleason argued each species changes gradually and independently along environmental gradients, so groupings are largely by chance.

definition.text: Stephen Hubbell's theory that species in a community are functionally equivalent and their numbers change through random births and deaths.

facts.text: Equivalent species undergo ecological drift: populations fluctuate randomly while the community's total number of individuals stays constant.

definition.text: A group of species that use the same resources, or use different resources in similar ways.

facts.text: Members of a guild compete because they share resources.
Guild members need not share the same niche or be closely related.
The number of guilds in an ecosystem is called its disparity.

definition.text: The ways different species affect each other, classed by whether each side gains, loses or is unaffected.

facts.text: They include competition, predation, parasitism, mutualism and commensalism.
Mutualism benefits both species, as with Rhizobium bacteria in nodules on legume roots.
In commensalism one species benefits and the other is unaffected, like an orchid growing on a tree.
In amensalism one species harms another while staying unaffected, as tadpoles do to snails by eating their algae.
Predation and parasitism benefit one species at the other's expense.
True neutralism, where neither species is noticeably affected, is rare because communities are so interconnected.

definition.text: An interaction in which organisms or species need the same resource, such as food, water or territory, that is in limited supply.

facts.text: Competition lowers the fitness of both sides, because each reduces what is available to the other.
Competition within a species is intraspecific; competition between different species is interspecific.
Intraspecific competition can regulate population size: as numbers grow, crowding leaves some individuals without enough resources.
It is one of the factors shaping community structure, species diversity and population dynamics.
In 1934 Georgii Gause proposed that species with the same ecological niche cannot coexist.
Cheetahs and lions share prey and harm each other, yet persist together despite the prediction that one should displace the other.

definition.text: The three ways competition works: interference, exploitation and apparent competition, from most to least direct.

facts.text: In interference (contest) competition organisms fight directly over scarce resources, as large aphids eject smaller ones from the best feeding sites.
In exploitation (scramble) competition one organism's use of a shared resource leaves less for others, without direct contact.
Apparent competition is not real competition: two prey species harm each other by sharing a predator.

definition.text: An indirect contest in which two unrelated prey species affect each other through a shared predator.

facts.text: If one prey species booms, its predator increases and then hunts both prey more heavily, so the other species declines.
Robert D. Holt coined the term in 1977.
Introduced snowshoe hares in Newfoundland may have shrunk the range of native arctic hares by boosting their shared lynx predator.
Conservation scientists see human introductions of predators or food subsidies such as garbage as an extreme, one-sided form of it.

definition.text: The evolution of differing traits in species that compete, because individuals most like their competitors fare worst.

facts.text: Individuals whose traits resemble competing species face stronger competition and leave fewer offspring.
Darwin's finches, found alone or together on the Galapagos Islands, are an example.

definition.text: An organism that breaks down dead organisms and releases their nutrients into the surrounding environment.

facts.text: 'Decomposer' names a role in an ecosystem, not a particular kind of organism.
Plants cannot move to find nutrients or digest other organisms, so they rely on decomposers to free nutrients from dead matter.
Decomposers include fungi and bacteria, which digest food outside their bodies, and invertebrates such as earthworms that digest it inside and release nutrients in their faeces.
Fungi are the main decomposers in forests, because only wood-decay fungi have enzymes to break down lignin and their hyphae can penetrate large pieces of wood.
By breaking down dead matter, decomposers return carbon to the air and recycle nutrients into forms plants can use.

definition.text: The breakdown of dead organic matter into simpler substances such as carbon dioxide, water, simple sugars and mineral salts.

facts.text: It is part of the nutrient cycle and essential for recycling the finite matter of the biosphere.
Abiotic decomposition happens by chemical or physical processes; biotic decomposition, or biodegradation, is done by living things, mainly microbes.
Plant matter decomposes in stages, starting with leaching of soluble compounds by water and physical fragmentation that gives decomposers more surface to attack.
Vertebrate bodies pass through five stages: fresh, bloat, active decay, advanced decay and dry remains.
Waterlogged soils slow decomposition, so carbon-rich sediments build up and act as a long-term carbon sink.
Ecosystems that lose biodiversity provide fewer services, including decomposing waste.

definition.text: How fast dead material breaks down, governed by the physical environment, the quality and amount of the material, and the microbes present.

facts.text: Decomposition is fastest in damp conditions with enough oxygen, and slow in very wet or very dry soils.
Labile compounds such as sugars break down fast, while recalcitrant ones such as lignin persist, so dead animals decay faster than leaves, and leaves faster than branches.
Tilling speeds decomposition by adding oxygen and exposing new organic matter to microbes.
Litter rich in lignin decomposes slowly, so low-lignin plant communities cycle nutrients faster.

definition.text: How efficiently energy passes from one trophic level to the next.

facts.text: Transfer between levels is generally inefficient: each level's net production is usually only about 10% of the level below.
Energy is lost through non-predatory death, egestion and respiration; halving at each of these three steps leaves about one-eighth, roughly ten percent.
It combines exploitation, assimilation and net production efficiencies, equal to consumer production divided by prey production.
Edible calories returned per calorie of cultivation energy are 18.1% for chicken, 6.7% for grass-fed beef and 0.9% for shrimp, versus 123% for potatoes, 250% for corn and 415% for soy.
So it is more energy-efficient to eat from lower trophic levels.
In 1999, 10.5% of the 28,400 terawatt-hours of energy used in the US went into food production.

definition.text: The rule of thumb that only about ten percent of food energy passing from one trophic level to the next is stored as new flesh.

facts.text: The rest is lost in transfer, used in respiration or lost through incomplete digestion.
It is credited to Raymond Lindeman (1942), though he did not call it a law and cited efficiencies from 0.1% to 37.5%.
In the standard example, of 10,000 J of sunlight plants take 100 J, a deer 10 J, a wolf 1 J, and a human eating the wolf 0.1 J.

title: Marine ecological efficiency
article: Ecological efficiency#Ecological efficiency in the marine environment

definition.text: The generally higher efficiency of energy transfer between trophic levels in the sea than on land.

facts.text: Transfer from phytoplankton to herbivorous zooplankton is estimated at about 20%, compared with 10% on land.
Phytoplankton biomass can turn over 100–300 times a year, while land plants turn over only 0.5 to 2.0 times.
Coastal upwelling zones may have as few as three trophic levels and support whales, while open oceans can have six and support only small tuna and squid at the top.

definition.text: A diagram showing the biomass or productivity at each trophic level of an ecosystem, with producers at the base.

facts.text: A pyramid of energy shows energy kept as new biomass at each level, a pyramid of biomass shows the living matter present, and a pyramid of numbers counts individuals.
Energy pyramids are normally upright, but biomass pyramids can be inverted in the sea and number pyramids when many beetles feed on one tree.
In a pond, the phytoplankton present at any moment weigh less than the fish and insects, because they reproduce fast but live briefly.
Only 1 to 2 percent of the Sun's energy is absorbed by photosynthesis and turned into food.
Charles Elton developed the pyramid of numbers in 1927; Bodenheimer expressed it in biomass in 1938, and the energy pyramid draws on Hutchinson and Lindeman (1942).

definition.text: The study of how the balance of energy and chemical elements shapes living things and their interactions in ecosystems.

facts.text: It focuses on mismatches between what organisms need and what their food contains: termites have a carbon:nitrogen ratio of about 5 yet eat wood with a ratio of 300–1000.
Plants and algae vary widely in their elemental make-up, whereas animals keep a nearly fixed composition, a trait called stoichiometric homeostasis.
Lake algae and detritus range in C:P ratio from 100 to 1000, while the zooplankton Daphnia stays near 80:1.
Nitrogen and phosphorus pollution from farming can boost stream producers and ripple up the food web.

title: Ecological succession

definition.text: The way the mix of species in an ecological community changes over time.

facts.text: There are two main kinds: primary succession, on newly created ground with no life, and secondary succession, after a disturbance such as fire destroys an existing community.
Succession is driven by feedbacks: growing plants create shade, add organic matter to soil and change nutrient supply, opening room for different plants.
Early-succession communities are dominated by fast-growing, well-dispersed species.
As a community approaches climax, species diversity, plant biomass and stability rise, while net primary productivity and nutrient cycling rates fall.
A tilled-up grassland is estimated to need at least 100 years, and potentially 1,400 years on average, to regain its earlier biodiversity.
Succession is shaped both by whether seeds can reach a site (dispersal limitation) and whether they can survive there (environmental filtering).
How much random chance, versus deterministic factors, steers succession is debated.

contested_note: Ecologists debate how far random events, rather than deterministic factors, set the path of succession.

definition.text: Succession that begins when life first colonizes an area with little or no living matter.

facts.text: It starts on surfaces such as newly exposed rock or sand, lava flows and freshly exposed glacial till.
Its stages run from pioneer species such as microorganisms, lichens and mosses, through grasses and small shrubs, to trees.

definition.text: In classical theory, the end point of succession, where the community is in steady balance with its environment and persists unless heavily disturbed.

facts.text: A climax community is described as having wide species diversity and complex food chains.
At climax, gross primary production is balanced by total respiration, and nutrient uptake from soil is balanced by nutrient return in litter fall.
Frederic Clements held that succession converges on a climate-determined stable climax; modern ecologists have largely abandoned this idea for nonequilibrium views.
Intermediate stages on the way to climax are called seral communities.

definition.text: A transition zone where two plant communities meet and blend.

facts.text: Examples include estuaries, lagoons, salt marshes, riparian zones and the zone between grassland and forest.
An ecotone can be narrow or wide, local or regional, and may show as a gradual blending or a sharp boundary.
Ecotones matter for mobile animals, which can use more than one set of habitats within a short distance.
The greater variety of plants and animals where communities meet is called the edge effect.

definition.text: A physical transition zone between two systems, where the environment changes along one or two physical or chemical factors.

facts.text: An ecocline can be a gradient in temperature (thermocline), chemistry (chemocline), salinity (halocline) or water density (pycnocline).
Ecoclines are less clear-cut and more stable than ecotones, so they hold higher plant species richness.

definition.text: A single linear path through a food web, usually starting with a producer such as grass or algae and ending with a top predator or decomposer.

facts.text: A food chain shows who eats whom by trophic level; a food web is the non-linear network formed when many food chains interconnect.
Its base is primary producers, which make organic compounds from sunlight or from inorganic chemicals; every other member is a consumer.
In dark places such as hydrothermal vents, chemosynthetic bacteria and archaea using hydrogen sulfide and methane form the base of the chain.
A simple example: a green plant eaten by a snail, eaten by a frog, eaten by a snake, eaten by an eagle.
When organisms die, decomposers and detritivores break their remains into simple nutrients returned to the soil for plants.
Food chains are used in ecotoxicology to trace how contaminants pass along and biomagnify.
Removing even one link can push other species toward extinction.

definition.text: The number of feeding links between a consumer and the base of its food chain.

facts.text: Generally only about ten percent of the energy at one trophic level passes to the next; the rest is used up in metabolism.
Food chains usually have no more than five trophic levels.
Eating lower in the chain gives more energy: a salad yields more energy per pound than an animal that ate lettuce.
Ecologists have proposed that chain length grows with ecosystem volume, is capped by energy loss at each level, or reflects habitat type.

definition.text: A species that plays a strong role in shaping the structure of its community.

facts.text: Foundation species can sit at any trophic level: producers, herbivores or predators.
Paul K. Dayton coined the term in 1972 for certain marine invertebrates and algae.
Corals, kelps, oysters, seagrasses, mangroves and forest trees help other organisms by creating habitat and easing physical stress such as waves and drying.
Studies removing creosote bush and eastern hemlock found species diversity rose afterwards, suggesting foundation species can sometimes limit diversity.

definition.text: A set of organisms in a community that share traits and do similar jobs, regardless of how closely related they are.

facts.text: Plant functional groups are called plant functional types; animal ones are called guilds and usually share a way of feeding.
Functional groups are identified by direct observation of behaviour and contribution, not from theory.

title: Functional redundancy

definition.text: The situation where several species in an ecosystem fill similar roles, acting as insurance if one is lost.

facts.text: A redundant species can take over the job of a similar species in the same functional niche.
Where redundancy is high, losing one species will not always reduce ecosystem function, so conserving the group matters more than any one species.
Whether conservation should protect particular species or functional traits is still debated.

contested_note: It is debated whether conserving specific species or functional traits better preserves ecosystem function.

title: Green world hypothesis

definition.text: The idea that the world stays green because predators keep down the herbivores that would otherwise eat the vegetation.

facts.text: It is also called the HSS hypothesis after Hairston, Smith and Slobodkin, who published it in 1960.
Sea otter studies support it: otters eat sea urchins, and without otters urchins nearly eliminate kelp forests, leaving urchin barrens.
The rival plant self-defense hypothesis says plants survive mainly through thorns, toxins and tough tissues.

contested_note: The plant self-defense hypothesis offers a competing explanation that plant defenses, not predators, keep herbivores from eating all vegetation.

definition.text: An animal adapted to eat plants, such as leaves, fruits or seeds, as the main part of its diet.

facts.text: Herbivores are primary consumers: they eat the carbohydrates plants make by photosynthesis, and carnivores in turn eat them.
Many rely on gut bacteria and protozoans to break down cellulose, which is much harder to digest than animal tissue.
Herbivory shapes plant diversity: abundant deer reduce plant species richness, while bison hold back dominant plants so others can flourish.
When predators decline, unchecked herbivores can over-forage and suppress plant communities.
Over-browsing by white-tailed deer in the US could cost forest restoration projects more than $750 million a year.
Some herbivory is mutualistic: seed dispersal and pollination feed the animal while helping the plant reproduce.

definition.text: The two main herbivore feeding strategies: grazers such as cows eat mostly grass, while browsers such as moose eat tree leaves and twigs.

facts.text: A land mammal counts as a grazer if at least 90% of its forage is grass, and a browser if at least 90% is tree leaves and twigs; in between is mixed-feeding.
Small herbivores pick high-quality forage, while larger ones are less selective.
Kleiber's law says larger animals need less food per unit of body weight than smaller ones.

definition.text: A plant trait that improves its survival or reproduction when animals feed on it.

facts.text: Defenses fall into tolerance, withstanding damage without losing fitness, and resistance, reducing how much damage is done.
Herbivores counter defenses by choosing which plants to eat, adapting their own bodies, or modifying the plant.
Many herbivores eat a mix of plants to balance nutrients and avoid too much of any one defensive chemical.

definition.text: An organism that cannot make its own food and instead gets its carbon from other organisms or their remains.

facts.text: Heterotrophs include most animals, all fungi, some bacteria and protists, and many parasitic plants.
In a food chain they are the consumers, while autotrophs, which make food from sunlight or inorganic chemicals, are the producers.
Detritivores are heterotrophs that eat dead plant and animal matter and feces.
Respiration by heterotrophic microbes releases much of the CO2 entering the atmosphere, which plants then reuse.
By mineralization they convert organic nitrogen, sulfur and phosphorus into inorganic forms plants can use, which is critical to plant survival and soil fertility.

definition.text: The food web of life in the sea.

facts.text: Its base is phytoplankton, single-celled algae and plant-like organisms; zooplankton that eat them form the second trophic level.
A typical ocean food chain runs phytoplankton, herbivorous zooplankton, carnivorous zooplankton, filter feeder, predatory vertebrate.
Forage fish sit in the middle of ocean food webs as the main prey of larger fish, seabirds and mammals.
Coastal waters cover about 8 per cent of the ocean but account for about half of all ocean productivity.
Microorganisms play much bigger roles in marine food webs than was once thought.
Ocean acidification damages pteropods and brittle stars at the base of Arctic food webs and threatens those webs from the bottom up.

definition.text: In the sea, the total mass of consumers can exceed that of the producers, turning the usual biomass pyramid upside down.

facts.text: This happens because phytoplankton grow and reproduce fast, so a small mass can sustain a high rate of primary production.
Because of this inversion, zooplankton make up most marine animal biomass.
Ocean producers are tiny, fast-reproducing phytoplankton, so a small mass yields high production, while land producers like mature forests need far more mass for the same output.
As a result zooplankton make up most marine animal biomass and link phytoplankton to the rest of the food web.

definition.text: The process by which whales carry nutrients from the ocean depths back up to the surface.

facts.text: Whales feed deep down where krill are found but return regularly to the surface to breathe.
It reverses the usual downward flow of nutrients in the ocean's biological pump, where marine snow sinks from surface to bottom.
In the Gulf of Maine whales carry more nitrogen through their feces than all the rivers in that system combined.
Whale feces are up to 10 million times richer in iron than seawater, feeding phytoplankton in the iron-poor Southern Ocean.

definition.text: An interaction between species in which each gains a net benefit.

facts.text: Examples include plants trading with mycorrhizal fungi, pollination of flowers, seed dispersal by fruit-eating animals, and corals living with zooxanthellae algae.
It contrasts with competition, where both lose fitness, and parasitism, where one benefits at the other's expense.
In mycorrhizae, the plant gives carbohydrates to the fungus in return mainly for phosphate; rhizobia fix nitrogen for legumes in return for carbohydrates.
Service-resource mutualisms such as pollination, cleaning symbiosis and seed dispersal by animals are common.
Mutualism can evolve from parasitism or commensalism, and can also break down again.
In Three Sisters farming, beans climb cornstalks while fixing nitrogen for the corn.

definition.text: The web of mutualistic links between plants and pollinators, which shows a similar structure across very different ecosystems and continents.

facts.text: Models suggest this structure reduces competition between pollinators and strengthens ecosystem stability.
Pollinators therefore survive harsh conditions together but collapse simultaneously once conditions pass a critical point.
These networks have a strikingly similar structure on different continents, even with entirely different species.
Network structure may shape how pollinator communities respond to harsher conditions.

definition.text: Mathematical models that describe how the populations of two mutualist species grow given the benefit each gets from the other.

facts.text: A simple form adapts the Lotka–Volterra equations, adding a positive term for the benefit of the partner species.
In 1989 David Hamilton Wright added saturation: benefits level off at high densities because of handling time.
Without saturation, modelled densities could grow without limit, which carrying capacity makes impossible.

definition.text: A close relationship in which one organism, the parasite, lives on or in another, the host, and harms it.

facts.text: Parasites range from protozoans that cause malaria to hookworms, lice, fungi such as honey fungus, and plants such as mistletoe.
Unlike decomposers that feed on dead matter, parasites feed on living hosts.
Almost all free-living animals host at least one parasite species; vertebrates host between 75,000 and 300,000 species of helminths.
Parasitic plants make up about one per cent of flowering plants and occur in almost every biome.
Most hosts carry few parasites, while a few hosts carry the great majority of them.
Parasitoid wasps and microbial pathogens are used as biological control agents in agriculture.

definition.text: The six main ways parasites exploit animal hosts: parasitic castration, direct transmission, transmission by being eaten, transmission by a vector, parasitoidism and micropredation.

facts.text: Vector-transmitted parasites rely on an intermediate host to carry them between their main hosts.
Parasitoids are insects that eventually kill their hosts, which puts them close to predators.
A micropredator feeds briefly on many hosts, which makes it well suited to carrying smaller parasites between them.

definition.text: The way hosts and parasites evolve together, changing their relationship over time.

facts.text: A parasite with a single host is pushed toward being more benign, even mutualistic, because it can reproduce longer if its host lives longer.
Competition between parasites tends to favour faster-reproducing, more virulent strains.
Hosts defend themselves with skin barriers, immune systems, grooming and plant chemical defenses.

definition.text: The tiny drifting organisms in oceans and lakes that make their own food by photosynthesis.

facts.text: They need sunlight, so they live in the sunlit surface layer of oceans and lakes.
They do about half of global photosynthesis and produce at least half of the oxygen, though they are only about 1% of global plant biomass.
Marine phytoplankton fix about 50 Pg of carbon a year in net primary production.
They form the base of marine and freshwater food webs and drive the biological pump that moves carbon to the deep sea.
They include cyanobacteria and protists such as diatoms; there are about 5,000 known marine species.
Their turnover takes days rather than decades, so they respond quickly to climate change; warming-driven stratification cuts nutrient supply and productivity.
Some studies indicate global phytoplankton density has decreased over the past century.

definition.text: The ratio of carbon to nitrogen to phosphorus, 106:16:1, shared by phytoplankton and the dissolved nutrients of the deep ocean.

facts.text: Alfred C. Redfield proposed that phytoplankton requirements control this ocean ratio, since they release nitrogen and phosphorus when remineralized.
It became a fundamental principle of marine ecology and biogeochemistry.
It is not universal: nitrogen fixation, denitrification and changing nutrient inputs can shift it.

definition.text: A group of organisms of the same species living in a particular place at a particular time.

facts.text: A population is usually described by who belongs to it, its size, the area it occupies and the time period studied.
Ecologists stress individuals interacting and competing in an area; the evolutionary view stresses genes and reproduction.
Populations of different species living and interacting together make up a community.
Large populations are rarely counted in full; methods such as the Lincoln index estimate total numbers from individuals observed.
Spatially separated populations of one species can be called a metapopulation.

definition.text: The study of how species populations change through births, deaths, immigration and emigration, and how they interact with their environment.

facts.text: Population size is the number of individuals; population density is how closely packed they are.
Change in numbers follows N1 = N0 + B − D + I − E: starting numbers plus births, minus deaths, plus immigrants, minus emigrants.
Carrying capacity is the largest population the environment's resources can sustain.
Population viability analysis, which predicts a species' long-term chance of persisting in a habitat patch, grew from this field and matters for conservation.
Fisheries and wildlife managers track three rates: recruitment, growth and mortality, including harvest mortality.
Population dynamics began with Malthus's model, in which a population in a constant environment grows or declines exponentially.

definition.text: The two most common population growth models: exponential, with a constant per-head growth rate, and logistic, where growth slows as numbers approach carrying capacity.

facts.text: Exponential growth assumes unlimited resources and no predation.
Monk parakeets released in the United States grew exponentially from 1975 to 1994, to about 55 times their 1975 numbers.
Verhulst and Gompertz refined Malthus's exponential model in the early 19th century.
In classic models r is the intrinsic growth rate and K the carrying capacity.

definition.text: A graph showing how many members of a population survive to each age.

facts.text: Type I curves, typical of K-selected species such as most mammals, show deaths mostly late in life.
Type II shows equal chance of death at any age; Type III shows heavy early losses, then good survival for those that pass a certain age.

definition.text: A population of populations that go extinct locally and recolonize, spread over patches of habitat of varying quality.

facts.text: The concept was introduced in 1969.
Patches are either occupied or empty, and productive source patches supply migrants to other patches.

definition.text: An interaction in which one organism, the predator, kills and eats another, its prey.

facts.text: Predation belongs to a family of feeding behaviours with parasitism and parasitoidism, and overlaps with herbivory when animals destroy seeds.
To feed, a predator must search for, pursue and kill its prey, weighing costs and benefits at each step.
Predators affect ecosystems indirectly too, by changing herbivore behaviour, as wolves do for riverside vegetation and sea otters for kelp forests.
Predators can raise biodiversity by stopping any one species from becoming dominant; such predators are called keystone species.
Without predators a prey population can grow exponentially until it nears carrying capacity; predators limit prey by eating them and changing their behaviour.
Predator–prey interactions may explain population cycles such as those of lynx and snowshoe hares.

definition.text: The ways predators search for and capture prey, from sit-and-wait ambush to active chase.

facts.text: Sit-and-wait suits dense, mobile prey and low energy needs; wide foraging costs more energy and suits sparse or sedentary prey.
In social predation, groups such as wolves or hyenas cooperate to kill animals as large as buffalo.
Specialists such as the Eurasian lynx hunt few prey types, while generalists such as leopards take at least 100 species.

definition.text: The arms race in which predators and prey evolve adaptations that counter each other.

facts.text: Bats evolved echolocation to find insects, and some insects evolved the ability to hear those calls.
Prey defences include camouflage, mimicry and warning others of predators.

definition.text: The rate at which an ecosystem makes new biomass, often measured in grams per square metre per day.

facts.text: Productivity of plants and other autotrophs is primary productivity; that of animals and other heterotrophs is secondary productivity.
It depends on nutrient availability, temperature and water availability.
Swamps and marshes are listed as producing 2,500 gC/m²/yr of biomass.
Fertilizer nutrients can trigger algal blooms that raise primary production but make the ecosystem less stable.

definition.text: The creation of new biomass by consumers, such as animals, fungi and many bacteria, from the food they assimilate.

facts.text: It is driven by the transfer of organic material between trophic levels.
It can be estimated by methods including increment summation, removal summation, the instantaneous growth method and the Allen curve method.

title: Diversity–productivity relationship

definition.text: The long-running question of how the number of plant species in an ecosystem relates to how productive it is.

facts.text: Some research finds productivity rises with diversity, partly because more species makes it likelier a highly productive one is present.
Others find a unimodal relationship; a meta-analysis of 44 studies found it unimodal in all but one.
A 1999 study of European grasslands found productivity rose with diversity and then levelled off.

contested_note: Studies disagree whether productivity rises steadily with plant diversity or peaks at intermediate diversity.

definition.text: Succession that follows an event such as fire, harvesting or a hurricane that knocks back an existing ecosystem while leaving soil and some life in place.

facts.text: It is usually faster than primary succession because soil, seeds, roots and underground plant parts survive.
After wildfire in an oak–hickory forest, annual plants come first, then grasses and pioneers, then shrubs and young trees.
Over about 150 years such a forest returns to a stable climax community resembling the one before the fire.
Succession from Imperata grassland to secondary forest raises soil carbon stocks.
Some species need fire: knobcone pine cones open only when heated by forest fires.

definition.text: A mixture of minerals, organic matter, gases, water and organisms that together support plant and soil life.

facts.text: Soil is a three-phase system: a solid matrix of minerals and organic matter, pores holding gases, and water carrying dissolved substances.
It serves as a habitat, a nutrient and waste recycler, a regulator of water quality and the atmosphere, and a medium for plant growth, making it a key provider of ecosystem services.
A gram of soil can hold billions of organisms from thousands of species, mostly microbes and largely unexplored.
A recent study suggested soil is home to 59 ± 15% of the species on Earth.
Texture, set by the proportions of sand, silt and clay, is the most important physical property for services such as crop production.
Civilizations have prospered or declined according to the availability and productivity of their soils.

definition.text: The typical make-up of soil: about half solids and half pore space.

facts.text: A typical soil is about 45% mineral and 5% organic matter, with pores split equally between water and gas.
Mineral and organic content is roughly constant in the short term, while water and gas trade places as one rises and the other falls.
In soil pores CO2 may reach 10 to 100 times its 0.04% atmospheric concentration, because roots and microbes consume oxygen and release CO2.

definition.text: A soil's ability to hold positively charged nutrient ions from the soil water and release them later to plant roots.

facts.text: Charges on clay and humus particles let them hold cations or anions on their surfaces.
Cation exchange buffers soil pH, alters soil structure and cleans percolating water by holding both useful and harmful cations.
It is measured in milliequivalents per 100 grams of dry soil (meq/100 g).
Base saturation is the share of exchange sites held by base-forming cations such as calcium and magnesium.

definition.text: A measure of how acidic or alkaline a soil is.

facts.text: In practice soil pH ranges from 3.5 to 9.5, since values beyond those extremes are toxic to life.
A soil's buffering capacity, its resistance to pH change, rises with cation exchange capacity; pure sand has almost none.

definition.text: The decline of soil's ability to function, through acidification, contamination, desertification, erosion or salination.

facts.text: Erosion is caused by water, wind, ice and gravity, and several kinds can occur at once.
Desertification in dry regions is often caused by poorly adapted human activities such as overgrazing or excess firewood harvesting; drought alone is a common misconception.
Salination is a build-up of salts that degrades the agricultural value of soils and vegetation.
At low levels, soil organisms can treat contamination, mainly through microbial enzymes.

definition.text: A horizontal layer of soil whose features, composition and age differ from the layers above and below.

facts.text: Soil formation is often marked by a B horizon, where clay, humus, iron oxide, carbonate and gypsum washed down from above accumulate.

definition.text: The study of the life in soil, from bacteria and fungi to earthworms and burrowing mammals, and what it does.

facts.text: Soil organisms break down organic matter, releasing nutrients for plants, which shapes fertility, soil structure and carbon storage.
Nutrients held in the bodies of soil organisms are protected from leaching, especially nitrogen and phosphorus.
A teaspoon of productive soil holds 100 million to 3 billion bacteria; a gram of garden soil can hold around 700 km of fungal hyphae.
Earthworms, ants and termites act as ecosystem engineers, mixing soil, improving water infiltration and enriching it with nutrients.
Saprotrophic fungi decompose dead matter into humus and mineral nutrients such as nitrate and phosphate.
Much about how soil populations function and interact is still unknown.

definition.text: The conversion of nitrogen from the air into nitrogen compounds living things can use, carried out by certain bacteria.

facts.text: It is done by free-living bacteria such as Azotobacter and cyanobacteria, or by rhizobia living in root nodules of legumes such as peas and beans.
Nitrogen-fixing bacteria play a decisive role in early soil formation.
Fixation must happen before plants can take up atmospheric nitrogen.
Lightning fixes between 5 and 10 billion kg a year, but most fixation is done by bacteria called diazotrophs.

definition.text: The step of the nitrogen cycle in which soil bacteria turn ammonium from decaying proteins into nitrates that plants can take up.

facts.text: Bacteria such as Nitrosomonas do this as autotrophic nitrifiers, making their own carbohydrate without photosynthesis.
It is an important step of the nitrogen cycle in soil, carried out with oxygen by small groups of bacteria and archaea.
Bacteria such as Nitrosomonas turn ammonia into nitrite, and others such as Nitrobacter turn nitrite into nitrate.
Converting ammonia matters because ammonia gas is toxic to plants.

definition.text: Processes in oxygen-poor soil that turn nitrates and nitrites back into nitrogen gas or nitrous or nitric oxide, returning nitrogen to the air.

facts.text: It is done mainly by anaerobic or facultatively anaerobic bacteria such as Pseudomonas.
Too much denitrification depletes soil nitrogen and fertility, and excess nitrogen fertilizer can cause it.
Bacteria such as Pseudomonas and Paracoccus do it in low-oxygen conditions such as waterlogged soils, using nitrate in place of oxygen to respire.
Because it removes nitrate and reduces leaching to groundwater, it can be used to treat sewage and high-nitrogen animal waste.

definition.text: A partnership between a fungus and plant roots that benefits both.

facts.text: The fungus takes carbohydrates from the root and in return supplies the plant with nitrogen, phosphorus and moisture.
Fungi either sheath the root (ectomycorrhizae) or enter root cells as arbuscules (arbuscular mycorrhizae).
Most tree species and many crops have mycorrhizae, but the cabbage family does not.
Chemical signalling between plants through shared mycorrhizal networks remains a matter of conjecture.

definition.text: The ability of soil to support plant growth and give steady, good-quality crop yields.

facts.text: A fertile soil supplies essential nutrients and water in adequate amounts and is free of toxic substances.
Helpful properties include enough depth for roots, good drainage and aeration, organic-rich topsoil, and a pH of 5.5 to 7.0.
Irrigating with salty, alkaline or acidic water can strip useful salts or build up harmful ones, cutting fertility; about 18% of the world's cropland is irrigated.
Soil organic matter and fertility are significantly correlated.

definition.text: The three main plant nutrients added as fertilizer, nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, which are always listed in a fertilizer's analysis.

facts.text: Bioavailable phosphorus is the nutrient most often lacking, especially in humid tropical soils.
A 10-10-15 fertilizer contains 10 percent nitrogen, 10 percent available phosphorus (P2O5) and 15 percent water-soluble potassium (K2O).
Inorganic fertilizers are more concentrated and immediately available to plants than organic ones.

definition.text: The loss of soil fertility when the things that make soil fertile are removed and not replaced.

facts.text: It leads to poor crop yields and is becoming a global problem.
Causes include overly intensive cultivation, over-tillage, overuse of nutrient inputs that mines the soil nutrient bank, and salinization.
Fertile soil is being depleted in many African farming regions, especially the Sahel under high population pressure.

title: Dark earths

definition.text: Dark, carbon-rich, highly fertile soils, many of them created or enriched by human soil management.

facts.text: Amazonian Dark Earth was created deliberately by Indigenous communities and contrasts sharply with the poor weathered soils around it.
In Ghana and Liberia, combining different wastes produces African Dark Earths rich in calcium, phosphorus and carbon.
The size of pre-1492 Amazonian societies, and Dark Earth's role in them, are continually debated.

contested_note: Scholars debate the size of pre-Columbian Amazonian societies and how far Dark Earth shaped them.

definition.text: The organic part of soil: plant and animal remains at various stages of decay, soil microbes, and substances they make.

facts.text: It improves soil structure, water retention, soil biodiversity, pollutant retention, pH buffering and nutrient cycling.
It raises fertility by holding nutrients on exchange sites and slowly releasing nitrogen, phosphorus and sulfur as it mineralizes.
It is usually estimated to be 58% carbon, so measured soil organic carbon often stands in for it.
Microbes decompose plant litter into minerals plants can absorb (mineralization), while part becomes stable humus.
Organic matter builds up where cold or wet conditions slow decomposers, and breaks down fast in hot, rainy tropical climates.
About 70% of global soil organic carbon lies below 20 cm depth.

definition.text: Organic matter that soil organisms have broken down to the point where it resists further decay.

facts.text: Humus is usually five percent of soil or less by volume, yet it is an essential nutrient source and improves soil texture.
Its cation and anion exchange capacity is many times greater than that of clay on a dry-weight basis.
Humic substances are classed as fulvic acid, humic acid and humin, in order of rising molecular weight and resistance to microbes.

title: Soil carbon pool
article: Soil organic matter#Function in carbon cycling

definition.text: The large store of carbon held in the world's soils, a key part of the global carbon cycle.

facts.text: The global soil carbon pool is estimated at 2,500 gigatons, 3.3 times the 750-gigaton atmospheric pool and 4.5 times the 560-gigaton biotic pool.
Organic carbon, mostly as soil organic matter, accounts for about 1,550 gigatons; carbonates make up the rest.
Soil can act as a carbon sink through sequestration or a source through greenhouse gas emissions, depending on outside factors.

title: Mineral-associated organic matter
article: Soil organic matter#SOC distribution with depth

definition.text: Soil organic matter bound to mineral surfaces or locked in aggregates, which protects it from decomposers.

facts.text: It can persist for centuries, while particulate organic matter, mostly little-decomposed plant remains, lasts only years to decades.
Mineral influences dominate deeper soil carbon, helping explain why more carbon is stored at depth.

definition.text: An ecosystem found on land, such as tundra, taiga, forest, grassland or desert.

facts.text: Land ecosystems differ from aquatic ones by having soil rather than water at the surface, and plants extending above it.
