Water availability varies widely on land, and temperatures swing more by day and season than in water.
Terrestrial ecosystems cover 144,150,000 km², or 28.26% of Earth's surface.
Sustainable Development Goal 15 targets their conservation, restoration and sustainable use.

title: Trophic cascade

definition.text: A chain of indirect effects through a food web that follows when one feeding level is suppressed, which can reshape a whole ecosystem.

facts.text: In a top-down cascade, predators cut prey numbers or change prey behaviour, freeing the level below; removing top predators lets consumers overrun producers.
Removing fish-eating fish from a lake can turn the water from clear to green as phytoplankton flourish.
Where sea otters were hunted out, sea urchins increased and kelp declined.
Overfishing of Atlantic cod in the Baltic Sea let its prey, sprat, take over, which then reduced the copepods sprat eat.
Aldo Leopold first described the mechanism after seeing deer overgraze mountains once wolves were exterminated.
Yellowstone's wolf reintroduction is popularly cited as a cascade, but the ecosystem is too complex and open to be a straightforward example.
That cascades exist is not controversial, but how widespread they are has long been debated.

contested_note: Ecologists agree trophic cascades exist but have long debated how widespread they are.

title: Terrestrial trophic cascades

definition.text: The debate over whether trophic cascades on land are as strong as those in lakes, streams and seas.

facts.text: The earliest documented cascades were all aquatic, leading to speculation that cascades are mainly an aquatic phenomenon.
A 2002 meta-analysis found cascades generally weaker on land, with smaller changes in plant biomass.
A 2009 study found many tree species were heavily affected by the loss of an apex predator.
Critics note real food webs blur trophic levels through omnivory, diet changes with growth and outside resource inputs.

contested_note: Studies disagree on whether land ecosystems show cascades as strong as aquatic ones.

definition.text: The movement of energy through the living things of an ecosystem.

facts.text: Producers turn sunlight into stored chemical energy as glucose through photosynthesis; respiration reverses this, releasing energy.
Organisms are organized into producers and consumers in food chains, and those chains into trophic pyramids.
Secondary production by herbivores and decomposers depends on primary productivity.
Primary producers fix carbon at similar rates across ecosystems, but how energy moves to higher levels differs.
Energy flow depends on primary productivity together with temperature, water and light.

definition.text: Two or more species reciprocally shaping each other's evolution through natural selection.

facts.text: Flowering plants and insects have coevolved for over 100 million years, creating a complex network of interactions; the earliest bees appeared in the early Cretaceous.
Hummingbirds and bird-pollinated flowers show a mutualism in which nectar, colour, shape and blooming time match the birds' diet, vision, bills and breeding season.
Hosts and parasites enter an arms race; the Red Queen hypothesis predicts that sexual reproduction lets a host stay just ahead of its parasite.
Predators and prey, and herbivores and plants, impose mutual selective pressures that produce arms races and anti-predator adaptations.
Coevolution can be pairwise or diffuse among a guild of species, and under the geographic mosaic theory it differs between populations depending on location and community ecology.
Humans induce it: disease-resistant crop varieties bred since the 1940s favored rapid evolution in pathogens that overcame the plant defences.
Norgaard and Gowdy applied it to economics and society, arguing that the economy, society and the environment are linked in a coevolutionary relationship.

definition.text: Close, long-term interaction between species, of six types distinguished by the benefit or harm each partner receives.

facts.text: The six types are mutualism, commensalism, parasitism, neutralism, amensalism and competition.
Commensalism benefits one organism and neither helps nor harms the other, as a remora does with a manatee.
Amensalism harms one organism with no effect on the other, for example antibiotic production by microbes or hoofed mammals trampling grass.
The term was long debated over whether it should denote only mutualism, which produced two classifications of interactions: by duration, and by strength of effect.

definition.text: Species interactions that are not feeding relationships, such as habitat modification, mutualism and competition for space.

facts.text: They can indirectly change food web topology and trophic dynamics by affecting the species in the network and the strength of trophic links.
Researchers argue that trophic and non-trophic interactions should be integrated in ecological network analysis.
The few empirical studies cover a limited number of coastal systems, so it is unclear how far the findings generalize.

definition.text: A heterotroph that gets nutrients by eating detritus: decomposing plant and animal parts and faeces.

facts.text: Detritivores ingest lumps of matter, unlike bacteria, fungi and protists, which are decomposers that absorb nutrients at a molecular scale (saprotrophic nutrition).
They perform the first stage of remineralization by fragmenting dead plant matter, so decomposers can do the second stage.
Typical detritivores include millipedes, springtails, woodlice, dung flies, slugs, earthworms and sea cucumbers.
Their activity is why plant litter does not accumulate in nature, and with decomposers they return carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, calcium and potassium to the soil.
Feeding on sediment, some detritivores incidentally concentrate toxic pollutants.
Fungi and bacteria had not yet evolved the ability to digest lignin in the Carboniferous, so large deposits of dead plant tissue built up and later became fossil fuels.

definition.text: A large land or water area defined by its environmental resources and containing a geographically distinct assemblage of natural communities and species.

facts.text: WWF's definition requires that communities share most of their species and dynamics, share similar environmental conditions, and interact ecologically in ways critical to their long-term persistence.
Boundaries rarely form abrupt edges; they are bounded by ecotones and mosaic habitats, and most ecoregions contain habitats that differ from their assigned biome.
Bailey's algorithmic system gives priority to climate and ecological criteria; the WWF system, built for biodiversity conservation planning, gives priority to the distribution of species assemblages.
The WWF framework first set out 867 terrestrial ecoregions in 14 biomes and 8 biogeographic realms; a 2017 update with satellite imagery reduced the count to 846 and later 844.
Marine ecoregions of the world number 232, grouped into 62 provinces and 12 realms; the freshwater map of 2008 has 426 ecoregions.
The Global 200 is WWF's list of priority ecoregions for conservation.

definition.text: A minor atmospheric gas that is an active part of the planetary nitrogen cycle and a long-lived greenhouse gas.

facts.text: It is the third most important greenhouse gas for global warming and has been a major ozone-depleting substance.

Per molecule over 100 years it traps 265 times as much heat as CO2, but its concentration is under one thousandth of CO2's, so its greenhouse contribution is less than one third that of carbon dioxide.
Atmospheric abundance has grown more than 20% from about 270 ppb in 1750, surpassing 330 ppb in 2017, and is rising about 1 ppb per year.
About 40% of emissions are human-caused, with growth chiefly from expanding agriculture; annual human emissions equal about 3 billion tonnes of CO2 in greenhouse effect.
Microbes produce it by nitrification, denitrification and nitrifier denitrification.

definition.text: The community of organisms living all or part of their lives in the soil, and how their feeding links move energy through it.

facts.text: Plant roots feed the web underground by exuding acids, sugars and enzymes into the rhizosphere, and decomposers such as bacteria and fungi end each chain by breaking dead matter into simple nutrients.

Soil organisms range from under 0.1 mm (nematodes) to over 2 mm (earthworms), so small ones are extracted dynamically, for example with a Berlese funnel for arthropods and a Baermann funnel for nematodes.

Soil ecologists found that omnivory is common and that long, complex food chains stay resistant to drying, freezing and fumigation, contradicting May's models that predicted complexity destabilizes webs.
Litter transformers such as isopods enrich their own faecal pellets with microbes and re-eat them, a mutualism called an external rumen that top-down or bottom-up control cannot describe.

title: Food web representations
article: Soil food web#Types of food webs

definition.text: Food webs are drawn three ways: topological webs, flow webs and interaction webs.

facts.text: Topological webs are non-quantitative maps of which organisms eat which; they are compared by chain length and connectivity.
Flow webs add quantitative carbon or nutrient transfer, built from the biomass of each functional group, usually in kg carbon per hectare, assuming each group is in equilibrium.
Interaction webs show how one group influences another, including indirect effects, such as a predator of root herbivores benefiting the plant roots.
Community matrix models describe each link with Lotka-Volterra equations plus biomass and feeding data, and can show how small changes affect web stability.
